title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice designing sequential circuits and use transistors. Two independent hexadecimal digits were displayed on a dual seven segment display using a single decoder module and time multiplexing. A scanning module driven at 8 Hz swept the keypad rows and read the columns, lighting on-board LEDs to indicate which keys were pressed.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice designing sequential circuits and use transistors. Two independent hexadecimal digits were displayed on a dual seven segment display using a single decoder module and time multiplexing. A scanning module driven at 8 Hz swept the keypad rows and read the columns, lighting on-board LEDs to indicate which keys were pressed.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Time Multiplexed Display
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 48 MHz. A counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to 100hz. That blinking frequency was used to toggle the power between the seven segment displays. The design was tested using an automatic test bench to demonstrate that the correct signal was passed when the display was flipped between digits.


Keypad Scanner
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 48 MHz. counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to 8hz, and toggle a 4-state FSM such that each state was entered twice a second (2hz). The keypads output was read using inputs and then inverted due the active low behavior of the keypad.


Testing
Testbenches were written for the scanner and top level module to demonstrate that the state transitions happened correctly. The oscilliscope was also used to verify the circuitry performed as expected.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram


Show block diagram




Figure 1: Top level block diagram of the Verilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of the design. The top level module includes 3 submodules which contain the HSOSC, counter with muxing logic, scanner module, and display logic.


Schematic


Show seven segment display schematic




Figure 2: Schematic of the multiplexed seven segment display circuit. All FPGA pins in this circuit are configured in 100 kΩ pull-up mode.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from 2 PNP transistors from the 3.3 V pin. The FPGA pins toggle between these power pins, and ground each segment to light it. 100 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Show keypad scanner schematic




Figure 3: Schematic of the keypad scanner circuit.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from the 3.3 V pin, and the FPGA pins ground each segment to light it. 1 kΩ series resistors limit the on-board LED currents, and 150 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Display Current and Segment Resistor Calculations
The display is an HDSP-5721, a two digit common anode seven segment display. Its datasheet has a typical forward voltage of \(V_F = 2.0\text{ V}\) per segment at 20 mA.
Each segment is in series between the anode and an FPGA pin, with a \(100\,\Omega\) series resistor. The segments are driven from 3.3 V through a 2N3906 PNP transistor. The equation for the circuit is \(V_{cc} = V_{EC(sat)} + V_F + I_F R\). Taking \(V_{BE(sat)} = 0.25\text{ V}\) for the 2N3906, \(V_F = 2.0\text{ V}\) leaves 1.05 V across the resistor:
\[
I_F = \frac{V_{cc} - V_{BE(sat)} - V_F}{R}
    = \frac{3.3 - 0.25 - 2.0}{100\,\Omega}
    = \frac{1.05\text{ V}}{100\,\Omega} = 10.5\text{ mA}
\]
Because the two digits are time multiplexed, each segment is lit for half of each multiplexing period, so the average current per segment is \(I_{avg} = I_F / 2 = 5.25\text{ mA}\). This is under the max current rating of the anode.


PNP Anode Driver Calculations
Each common anode is switched by a 2N3906 PNP. The emitter is 3.3 V, the collector drives one digit. The base is driven by a \(330\,\Omega\) resistor from an FPGA pin.
If all seven segments are lit at once, the total current drawn is 73.5 mA, which is less than the maximum 200mA Continuous Collector Current.
\[
I_C = 7 \times 10.5\text{ mA} = 73.5\text{ mA}
\]
With an emitter-base saturation voltage of \(V_{EB(sat)} = 0.8\text{ V}\), the base current is
\[
I_B = \frac{V_{cc} - V_{BE(sat)}}{R_B}
    = \frac{2.5\text{ V}}{330\,\Omega} = 7.6\text{ mA}
\]


NPN Open Drain Keypad Driver Calculations
Each row is driven through a 2N3904 NPN. The emitter is grounded, the collector drives the row, and the base is driven through a \(470\,\Omega\) resistor from an FPGA pin.
With \(V_{OH} = 3.3\text{ V}\) and \(V_{BE(sat)} = 0.8\text{ V}\), the base current is
\[
I_B = \frac{V_{OH} - V_{BE(sat)}}{R_B}
    = \frac{2.5\text{ V}}{470\,\Omega} = 5.3\text{ mA}
\]

Figure 4 shows the QuestaSim results for the top level testbench. The display signals can be seen toggling between the switch inputs which confirms that the module functions as expected.

Shortcomings
I fell short on the transistor calculations. I don’t totally understand how transistors work. I had to ask for help on what values to use.

This lab took approximately 15 hours.

Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text: In lab 3, a keypad scanner feeding a time multiplexed dual seven segment display on the iCE40 UP5K fpga. When a new key is pressed on the keypad, the new key press shifts into the right digit, old digit shifts left. This lab helped build skills involing FSM design, synchronizing and debouncing inputs.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text: In lab 3, a keypad scanner feeding a time multiplexed dual seven segment display on the iCE40 UP5K fpga. When a new key is pressed on the keypad, the new key press shifts into the right digit, old digit shifts left. This lab helped build skills involing FSM design, synchronizing and debouncing inputs.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
Input synchronizers were used on all outside inputs to the fpga (reset, keyboard columns). A debouncer fsm waits for a set amount of time based on a variable flip_bit to debounce the 4 column signals from the keyboard. A scanner toggles rows to check for key presses using a 48 MHz HSOSC divided by 480,000.
A keypad decoder tells us what key is being pressed, and a keypad reader fsm determines when to update the display based on the keypad. The two digits are display on a reused module from Lab 2, which is multiplexed at 100 hz. Currently, no solution has been made to capture multiple key presses simultaineously, although solutions such as an additional state in the keypad reader have been proposed.
Each module that was not used in lab 2 has a testbench that expresses all FSM states or input to combinational logic.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram






Figure 1: Block diagram of top-level design, showing the input synchronizers and debouncers, keypad decoder, keypad reader, scanner, and display logic.



In this diagram we can see the general layout of the circuit. Synchronizer modules are present on all inputs to the fpga. A debouncer is placed on the columns in order to prevent switch bouncing from the keyboard. The Keypad Decoder tell us what key is being pressed. While the Keypade Reader module choses when to update the display, and feeds the data to the display module.


Schematic






Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit, showing the matrix keypad with 1 kΩ column pull-ups and transistor row drivers, and the HDSP-5721 dual seven segment display with 100 Ω segment resistors and transistor digit drivers. Note: Vdd = 3.3V



In this schematic, we see the general circuit layout for the lab. The keyboard has pull-ups on the column inputs, and row drivers. The display transistors and resistors are also shown. The schematic for this lab is effectively the same as lab 2.


State transition diagram






Figure 3: State transition diagram of the keypad reader FSM, showing the SCAN, PRESS, and HOLD states.



States:
SCAN: Allows the scanner to scan the rows until it detects a column pressed.
PRESS: The current key is stored in d0, and the old d0 goes to d1.
HOLD: Remains held until the all keys in the row are released.


Calculations
The scanner goes to the next row once every 480,000 cycles of the 48 MHz HSOSC clock:
\[
f_{row} = \frac{48\text{ MHz}}{480{,}000} = 100\text{ Hz}
\] \[
T_{row} = \frac{1}{100\text{ Hz}} = 10\text{ ms}
\]
Each row is driven for 10 ms before the scanner moves on. A 40 ms sweep is short compared to a typical human key press, so every press is seen on at least one full sweep.
The debounce time waits for \(2^{17}\) cycles at 48 MHz, which equates to a wait time of 2.7 ms. Switch bounces do not last this long on average.
The display resistors values and transistor configuration are identical the Lab 2. See Lab 2 writeup for reference.

text:
Results and Discussion
All profiency requirements were met on the board, however it lacks a way to detect more than one keypress at a time.

Figure 6: QuestaSim simulation of the debouncer.

Conclusion
The final design successfully detected all keypad presses without double presses from bouncing. In total, I spent 13-15 hours on this lab.

text:
Lab 3 AI Prototype

Model
The model used was Opus 5.5, the newest and most powerful frontier model at this time.


Prompt
Target device: Lattice iCE40 UP5K FPGA with internal high-speed oscillator (~20 MHz).

Write synthesizable SystemVerilog to scan a 4x4 matrix keypad and display the last two hex keys pressed on a dual 7‑segment display. Implement:

A clock divider that derives a scan clock on the order of 100–200 Hz from the internal oscillator.
A keypad scanning controller that iterates one active‑low column at a time and samples active‑low rows, registering at most one key per press (debounce‑by‑design), ignoring additional presses while any key is held, and allowing a new registration only after release.
A top level that updates two hex digits (older and most recent) when a new key is registered and drives a time‑multiplexed two‑digit 7‑segment display without visible flicker and with balanced brightness.
Use idiomatic SystemVerilog (e.g., logic, always_ff, enumerated states for FSMs). Provide clean module boundaries and keep all state synchronous. Include brief comments explaining the design choices.


Process






Figure 9: Summary of the steps Claude took while generating the AI prototype.



Claude took some interesting steps during its response. Most interestingly, it download verilator in order to simulate and debug its own code before giving it to me. This already gives me extreme confidence that this code will compile and run when I put it in Questa.


Simulation






Figure 10: QuestaSim simulation of the AI-generated prototype.



When simulated in Questa, the code showed clean transitions of the display from one digit to another. I would say an overall critique is overcomplex logic and names in the verilog. Also that the AI instaiated all the logic in a core, which I think is less configurable than just doing the lower modules in the top. The verilog generated by this model is included in the github.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In lab 4, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was programmed to play music through an 8-ohm speaker. The speaker was driven by a LM386 audio amplifier. Musical notes were store as a list of pitches (Hz) and durations (ms), which the microcontroller interpreted to program timer peripherals in order to create a wave of the same pitch.
This lab developed skills such as reading datasheets and creating register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In lab 4, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was programmed to play music through an 8-ohm speaker. The speaker was driven by a LM386 audio amplifier. Musical notes were store as a list of pitches (Hz) and durations (ms), which the microcontroller interpreted to program timer peripherals in order to create a wave of the same pitch.
This lab developed skills such as reading datasheets and creating register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The TIM16 timer peripheral was configured to create a PWM and overflows were counted to keep track of the notes duration.
System clock was set to MSI. In the APB2 bus, the prescaler was set to 3, which gave a input frequency of 1MHz to the timer.
The timer was set to PWM mode 1, which sets Channel 1 to active as long as \(TIM16_{CNT}<TIM16_{CCR1}\), else it is inactive.
The microcontroller read the overflow flag to keep track of the amount of clock overflows, then changes to the next note after a amount of overflows calculated from the notes duration.
The GPIO pin 6 was connected to TIM16 by writing registers MODER and AFRL. GPIO pin 6 (PA6) was externally connected to the LM386 audio amplifier. I used GPIO bank A on this design since it had the most external pins on the development board.
Defines were used to encode important addresses from the datasheet like the start of the GPIOA bank addresses. Structs were written to organize the register from the reference manual.
The design was tested using oscilloscopes to measure the frequency of the output by playing the Für Elise score.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Schematic






Figure 1: Schematic of the physical circuit, showing the MCU GPIO output driving the LM386 amplifier and the 8 Ω speaker.



Circuit schematic used was from Texas Instruments LM386 Low Voltage Audio Power Amplifier datasheet


Frequency and Duration Calculations
Timer clock and prescaler calculations
\[
f_{timer} = \frac{f_{clk}}{PSC + 1} = \frac{4 \text{Mhz}}{3 + 1} = 1\text{Mhz}
\]
Auto-reload value for a note of frequency \(f_{note}\)
\[
ARR = \frac{f_{timer}}{f_{note}} - 1
\]
The final output frequency of the timers signal is:
\[
f_{out} = \frac{f_{timer}}{ARR + 1}
\]
A note lasting \(t\) milliseconds last for \(n\) overflows, and the actual duration played is
\[
n = \frac{f_{note} * t}{1000}
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{n * (ARR + 1)}{f_{timer}}
\]

Example Calculations
Both examples use a 250 ms note.
Example 1: 220 Hz
\[
ARR = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{220\text{ Hz}} - 1 = 4545 - 1 = 4544
\]
\[
f_{out} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{4544 + 1} = 220.02\text{ Hz}
\]
\[
n = \frac{220\text{ Hz} * 250\text{ ms}}{1000} = 55
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{55 * 4545}{1000000\text{ Hz}} = 0.249975\text{ s} = 249.975\text{ ms}
\]
Example 2: 1000 Hz
\[
ARR = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{1000\text{ Hz}} - 1 = 999
\]
\[
f_{out} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{999 + 1} = 1000\text{ Hz}
\]
\[
n = \frac{1000\text{ Hz} * 250\text{ ms}}{1000} = 250
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{250 * 1000}{1000000\text{ Hz}} = 0.25\text{ s} = 250\text{ ms}
\]
Both example notes show that the system can create 220 Hz and 1000 Hz pitches within 1% accuracy.


Absolute Max/Min Frequency and Duration
Minimum frequency
TIM16 is a 16 bit timer, so the largest ARR is 65535. The lowest frequency is
\[
f_{min} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{65535 + 1} = 15.26\text{ Hz}
\]
Maximum frequency
The fastest we can make the timer output is with a cycle 2 ticks long, since we need one half to be on for the PWM signal to output.
\[
ARR + 1 = 2
\]
\[
f_{max} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{1 + 1} = 500000\text{ Hz} = 500\text{ kHz}
\]
Minimum duration
The minimum duration for a note is \(N = 1\) overflows
\[
t_{min} = \frac{1000}{f_{note}}\text{ ms}
\]
At the highest frequency, 500 kHz:
\[
t_{min} = \frac{1000}{500000}\text{ ms} = 0.002\text{ ms} = 2\text{ µs}
\]
Practically however, the minimum is 1 ms because durations are stored as integer milliseconds.
Maximum duration
\(n\) is computed with uint32_t, so \(f_{note} * t\) must stay below 4294967295. The longest note is possible at the lowest frequency, 16 Hz:
\[
t_{max} = \frac{4294967295}{16}\text{ ms} = 268435455\text{ ms} = 74.6\text{ hours}
\]
The timer is able to play fur elise all within 1% accuracy, since nearly all the notes fall close withing the range of 200-1000 Hz. This was additionally proven by calculating the error for every note in the song in a spreadsheet.(https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Ons0ZR9uOKoXykoLUrtP-t-9wVeZpt0yylUZN51Lkxk/edit?usp=sharing)

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Results and Discussion
All requirements for the lab were met. The songs were successfully played through the speaker circuit.

Shortcomings
In terms of shortcomings, the reference manual was intitially overwhelming, so much control+f was used to find features of interest.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, in Lab 4, a STM32L432KC was used to drive a 8 ohm speaker. The code was able to play notes accurately within 1% of the desired pitch and duration. The song “The Hall of the Mountain King” was also play, although it was translated into notes by AI because I am not a music major.
In total, I spent ~15 hours on this lab.

Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice basic FPGA programming. The on-board 48 MHz high-speed oscillator was divided down with a counter to blink an on-board LED at ~2.4 Hz. Four on-board switches drove a seven segment display and two additional on-board LEDs.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice basic FPGA programming. The on-board 48 MHz high-speed oscillator was divided down with a counter to blink an on-board LED at ~2.4 Hz. Four on-board switches drove a seven segment display and two additional on-board LEDs.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The on-board high-speed oscillator, HSOSC, from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library generated a 48 MHz clock. A counter divided that clock to drive one on-board LED, and combinational logic on the switch bits drove the other two.
The seven segment display module took 4 on-board switches as input and used case logic to select the segment pattern for the matching hexadecimal character.
Testbenches were written for every module, sweeping all inputs where that was feasible.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram


Show block diagram




Figure 1: Block diagram of the Verilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of the design. The top level module includes 3 submodules which contain the HSOSC, counter divider, and display logic.


Schematic


Show schematic




Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from the 3.3 V pin, and the FPGA pins ground each segment to light it. 1 kΩ series resistors limit the on-board LED currents, and 150 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Clock Divider Calculations
The HSOSC module runs at its default rate of \(f_{clk} = 48\text{ MHz}\). A counter counts to \(N = 20{,}000{,}000\) and resets, and the LED is on whenever the count is greater than \(\frac12 N\), so one full on/off cycle takes \(N\) clock cycles:
\[
f_{blink} = \frac{f_{clk}}{N} = \frac{48 \times 10^6\text{ Hz}}{20 \times 10^6} = 2.4\text{ Hz}
\]
That matches the rate specified in the lab guide and the rate observed on the board.


Seven Segment Circuit Calculations



Figure 3: Seven segment display circuit.





Figure 4: Forward current versus forward voltage for the seven segment display, taken from the HDSP-511A datasheet.


Each segment of the display is an LED with an absolute maximum current rating of 30 mA. The circuit was designed for a target current of \(I = 8\text{ mA}\).
Each segment of the display is driven from the 3.3 V pin, \(V_{cc} = 3.3\text{ V}\), and has a diode forward voltage of \(V_f = 1.8\text{ V}\) at the target current, as shown in Figure 4. The remaining voltage is dropped across the current-limiting series resistor:
\[
V_R = V_{cc} - V_f = 3.3\text{ V} - 1.8\text{ V} = 1.5\text{ V}
\]
Applying Ohm’s law across the resistor gives the required resistance:
\[
R = \frac{V_R}{I} = \frac{1.5\text{ V}}{8\text{ mA}} = 187.5\,\Omega
\]
A standard \(150\,\Omega\) resistor was used in the final design. It draws \(1.5\text{ V} / 150\,\Omega = 10\text{ mA}\) per segment, which is slightly above the 8 mA target but still well under the 30 mA maximum rating.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Results and Discussion

Testbench Simulation


Show testbench simulation




Figure 5: A QuestaSim simulation of the top level module, showing the switch inputs, the seven segment outputs, the internal oscillator, and the counter driving the LED.



Figure 5 shows the QuestaSim results for the top level testbench. Each switch input produced the expected seven segment pattern, and the LED output followed the counter, staying high for the top half of each cycle. The counter in the testbench was given a cycle length of ten clock cycles to demonstrate the reset functionality.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Conclusion
The design implemented all three LED behaviors. The on-board high-speed oscillator blinked the on-board LED, and the seven segment display showed all 16 outputs correctly. This lab took at least 20 hours.

Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
In lab 6, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to use its built-in serial peripheral interface to communicate with a DS1722 Digital Thermometer. The microcontroller also communicated with an ESP8266 32-bit Wi-Fi micro-controller chip over UART. The ESP8266 displayed html code that allowed users to change the state of an LED on the board, and change the resolution of the temperature measurement.
This lab developed skills regarding configuring serial protocols. It also built on the skill of writing register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
In lab 6, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to use its built-in serial peripheral interface to communicate with a DS1722 Digital Thermometer. The microcontroller also communicated with an ESP8266 32-bit Wi-Fi micro-controller chip over UART. The ESP8266 displayed html code that allowed users to change the state of an LED on the board, and change the resolution of the temperature measurement.
This lab developed skills regarding configuring serial protocols. It also built on the skill of writing register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Design
The SPI1 peripheral was configured to communicate with the DS1722 in full-duplex mode. This configuration uses four wires (CE, MISO, MOSI, SCLK).
The system clock on the microcontroller was set to PLL of 80 MHz. SPI1 is clocked from the APB2 bus, which was left at its default prescaler of 1, so \(f_{PCLK2} = 80\) MHz. The SPI clock is divided down from this by the baud rate control bits (BR) in SPI1_CR1:
\[
f_{SCLK} = \frac{f_{PCLK2}}{2^{BR+1}}
\]
With a baud rate setting of BR = 7 (0b111), the frequency of the SPI clock is
\[
f_{SCLK} = \frac{80\text{ MHz}}{2^{7+1}} = \frac{80\text{ MHz}}{256} = 312.5\text{ kHz}
\]
This is well below the DS1722’s maximum SCLK frequency of 5 MHz.
The PB3 pin was connected by GPIO to the LED. Pins PA9 and PA10 were used for the UART interface. I was provided pre-written drivers. The only important thing I had to do was to connect the MCU’s TX to the ESP8266’s RX, and vice versa.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Testing Methodology
Before flashing the MCU or connecting to the temperature or wifi sensors, the code was debugged in Segger Embedded Studio. I loaded the drivers and packages for my STM32L432KC MCU, and made sure the code was compiling and had no syntax errors. The SPI functionality was confirmed using an oscilloscope.

Oscilloscope
The ideal SPI protocol is described in the DS1722 datasheet, shown below.



SPI multiple byte burst transfer from the DS1722 datasheet (Figure 6).


To read from the temperature sensor, the address and data bytes are shifted MSB first into the serial data input (SDI) and out of the serial data output (SDO). As per the datasheet, any transfer requires the address of the byte to specify a write or a read, followed by one or more bytes of data. The temperature measurement is 2 bytes, meaning we will use a 3-byte burst to read 2 bytes from the address provided in the first byte. To read the temperature, we set the address to 0x01.



Oscilloscope capture of a 3-byte SPI read of the DS1722 temperature registers.


The SPI functionality was verified using an oscilloscope to measure all 4 wires. The waveforms confirm that the SPI setup is performing as expected. CE begins by going high. In the first byte, the MCU sends the address 0x01 on MOSI. In the second and third bytes, the MCU sends test data 0x56 and 0x73. The DS1722 shifts out the temperature on MISO, giving us the LSB (0x40), then MSB (0x14). This gives a reading of 0x1440, or 20.25 °C (68.45°F), which is a reasonable room temperature.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated GitHub repository.

Schematic



Schematic of the Lab 6 circuit, showing the MCU connected to the ESP8266 over UART, the DS1722 over SPI, and the LED on PB3.


The STM32L432KC connects to the DS1722 over SPI1 (SCLK on PA5, MISO on PA6, MOSI on PB5, CE on PB0), to the ESP8266 over UART (TX on PA9, RX on PA10), and drives the LED on PB3 through a 510 Ω resistor.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Results and Discussion
All requirements for the lab were met. The temperature sensor accurately displayed the temperature on the website. Input from the website was able to change the floating point resolution of the measurement.

Website



Webpage served by the ESP8266, with LED control buttons, temperature resolution buttons, and the current temperature reading.


The webpage served by the ESP8266 is shown above. Users can turn the LED on or off and select a temperature resolution from 8 to 12 bits. The page displays the current LED status, the selected resolution, and the temperature read from the DS1722.


Shortcomings
In terms of shortcomings, the reference manual for the SPI is difficult to understand. I would say I understand SPI to a high degree; however, I would likely benefit by creating a system that customizes the SPI configuration more, such as a multi-master or one-way communication system.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, in lab 6, SPI was used to interface with a temperature sensor. UART was used to send website info to an ESP8266. This allows people connected to the ESP8266’s wifi network to monitor the temperature sensor’s output with varying amounts of resolution.
In total, I spent ~13 hours on this lab.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Lab 6 AI Prototype

Model
I used Claude Opus 5.5 at High effort


Frontend Prompt
I’m making a web portal to interface with a temperature sensor. Create a HTML page that looks good and is intuitive to show the temperature, control an LED, and change the precision of the readout.

Process
I used Claude Code to make a branch of my code and integrate the HTML into the existing codebase.


Results
The AI-generated webpage is shown in Figure 1. Compared to my webpage in the Website section, it displays the temperature in both °C and °F with a color scale, uses a toggle for the LED with an indicator light, and labels each precision setting with its step size. It also adds a connection indicator and an auto-refresh option that updates the reading every 5 seconds.






Figure 1: AI-generated webpage, showing the temperature at 12-bit precision, the LED toggle, and the precision selector.






Embedded Prompt
Write me a C function to carry out a SPI transaction to retrieve a temperature reading from a DS1722 sensor. Use CMSIS libraries for the STM32L432KC.

Process
The code looks like it works, I loaded the AI prototype branch with the drivers integrated, and the website ran just like before. This indicates the drivers are functioning correctly.


Results
uint8_t ds1722ReadReg(uint8_t addr) {
    ceHigh();
    shortDelay();
    spiXfer(addr & 0x7F);              // address byte, A7 = 0 for read
    uint8_t val = spiXfer(0x00);       // dummy byte clocks the data out
    while (SPI1->SR & SPI_SR_BSY);     // let the last clock finish before dropping CE
    ceLow();
    shortDelay();
    return val;
}



Comparison
The LLM generated frontend web code better than low-level embedded C. I would say that for C, it might overcomplicate the drivers trying to make them more safe. For the application, I think my driver was more readable than the AI’s.


Reflection
I would rate the output quality very high. The generated code, although it functions identically, provides a much better UI, and a clean device driver. The LLM’s explanation of the driver was quite limited, but it left a fair amount of documentation in the driver that helps a lot.
